Front: Reason about work before writing code: If every value is equal, what is the result for n elements?
Back: n(n − 1) / 2. The output grows quadratically even though the counting algorithm is expected linear time.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for count_equal_pairs. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Before each iteration, counts describes exactly the processed prefix and pairs counts every matching pair entirely inside it. Adding counts[value] introduces exactly the pairs ending at the new position. No pair is missed or counted twice.

Front: Arrays, strings, and boundary handling: What should "ab a" produce?
Back: [('a', 1), ('b', 1), (' ', 1), ('a', 1)]. The two a runs are separate.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for compress_runs. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Before each new character, result contains every completed run and current/count describes the one unfinished run. A changed character closes exactly that run. The final append closes the only run not ended by a change.

Front: Hash maps: remember what a scan cannot: Can a set alone distinguish one occurrence from three?
Back: No. Both produce one membership entry. You need counts or another structure that records repeated membership.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for earliest_unique. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: After counting, each map entry is the exact frequency of its key. Scanning indices in increasing order means the first frequency-one item has no earlier qualifying item.

Front: Two pointers and monotone movement: Why is this approach unsafe for unsorted input?
Back: Moving right or left no longer predicts how the sum changes, so it can discard the optimal pair.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for closest_pair. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: When the sum is below target, all other pairs using the left endpoint and a smaller right endpoint are no closer than the current pair. The symmetric statement holds above target. Each discarded boundary therefore cannot hide a better unexplored pair.

Front: Sliding windows and reversible state: Why does the inner loop not imply O(n²) here?
Back: The left pointer advances at most n times across all outer iterations, not n times per iteration.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for longest_budget_window. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: After shrinking, the window is valid. Every removed left endpoint made a sum too large and cannot become useful by extending the right edge with more nonnegative costs. Across the scan, both pointers move only forward.

Front: Prefix sums for signed ranges: How many target-zero ranges are in [0, 0]?
Back: Three: each individual zero and the full two-element range.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for count_target_ranges. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Before processing each new prefix, seen contains exactly the prefixes at earlier boundaries. Each matching earlier prefix determines one nonempty range ending now. Querying first prevents a zero-length range when target is zero.

Front: Stacks and unresolved candidates: What is the answer for [5, 5, 6]?
Back: [2, 1, 0]. The second 5 does not resolve the first.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for next_warmer_wait. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: The stack temperatures are nonincreasing. Popping a prior day at the first warmer incoming day gives its nearest qualifying future day: any earlier warmer day would already have popped it. Every index is pushed once and popped at most once.

Front: Queues and shortest routes without weights: When is a plain BFS shortest-path guarantee valid?
Back: When each traversed edge has the same cost, commonly one step.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for nearest_exit_steps. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: FIFO processing ensures that all distance-d states are processed before distance-(d + 1) states. The first reachable boundary popped has minimum distance. Visited marking bounds each cell to one enqueue.

Front: Linked lists and safe pointer changes: Why should the original head eventually point to None?
Back: It becomes the new tail. Keeping its old next link could create a cycle.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for reverse_chain. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: At every iteration, previous is the head of the reversed processed prefix and current is the untouched suffix head. Saving following preserves the suffix before relinking. When current becomes None, the entire list is the reversed prefix.

Front: Binary search with explicit boundaries: What does lower_bound([3, 3], 4) return?
Back: 2, the insertion boundary after the last item.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for lower_bound. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Both updates preserve the boundary claims. Each update strictly shrinks the unresolved interval. When left equals right, every earlier element is too small and that boundary is the first possible qualifying index.

Front: Recursion as a contract for smaller work: Does two recursive calls always imply exponential time?
Back: No. If they visit disjoint portions of a tree, total work can still be linear in the total nodes.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for nested_total. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: For an empty list the result is zero. Assuming recursive calls correctly total each smaller nested list, adding those totals and the direct integers counts every integer exactly once.

Front: Tree DFS: return one fact, update another: Can the diameter lie entirely in the left subtree?
Back: Yes. Updating a global best at every node covers that case.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for tree_diameter. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Every path has a highest node where its two downward portions meet. Postorder computes the longest available downward portion on each side. Taking the maximum of their sums therefore considers an optimal path at its highest node.

Front: Tree BFS and level boundaries: Which can use O(n) queue space: a chain or a broad tree?
Back: A broad tree. A chain has at most one node in its queue at a time.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for level_means. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: At the start of a level, the queue contains precisely that level in order. Processing its captured width consumes all and only those nodes while appending their children. The invariant repeats for the next level.

Front: Binary search trees and inherited constraints: Does sorting a tree’s values prove that the original tree was a BST?
Back: No. Sorting discards structure. A strictly increasing inorder traversal would be a valid alternative check.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for valid_bst. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Each call receives exactly the ancestor constraints for its subtree. Rejecting a value outside them detects a violation; narrowing the interval for each child preserves every earlier constraint.

Front: Graphs: components and visited state: How many components does n = 4 with no edges contain?
Back: Four: each isolated vertex is its own component.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for component_count. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: A traversal follows exactly the edges reachable from its start, so it covers one complete component. No visited vertex starts another traversal. Every component eventually supplies one unseen start.

Front: Directed dependencies and topological order: What should a self-loop 2 → 2 imply?
Back: A cycle, so no topological ordering exists.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for dependency_order. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Every emitted vertex has zero incoming edges from unfinished work, so all of its prerequisites already precede it. A finite directed acyclic graph always has a zero-indegree vertex. If processing stalls early, the remaining subgraph contains a cycle.

Front: Heaps and keeping only the best candidates: For [5, 5, 2] with k = 2, what is the answer?
Back: 5. The two 5s occupy the first and second positions.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for kth_largest. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: After each input, the heap contains the largest min(k, processed_count) values seen so far. A newly pushed value can only displace the smallest retained candidate. At completion the root is the kth largest.

Front: Greedy choices need an exchange argument: Are (1, 3) and (3, 4) compatible here?
Back: Yes. Half-open intervals do not include their ending point.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for max_meetings. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Take an optimal solution’s first meeting. Replace it with the earliest finishing meeting; the replacement cannot overlap any later meeting that the original first meeting allowed. Repeat this exchange on the remaining compatible suffix.

Front: Backtracking: choose, explore, undo: Why does k = 0 have one selection rather than zero?
Back: There is exactly one way to select nothing: the empty selection.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for choose_tags. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Each selection has one unique increasing index sequence. The recursion follows exactly those sequences and cannot repeat them. Pruning only skips a suffix with fewer available items than remaining slots.

Front: Dynamic programming on one dimension: What is min_tokens([4, 6], 5)?
Back: -1: no exact combination exists.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for min_tokens. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Any solution for subtotal s ends in some allowed token c. Removing it leaves an optimal smaller problem; using a nonoptimal remainder could only increase the count. Trying every final token includes an optimal solution.

Front: Grid DP and careful memory reuse: Why can updating columns right-to-left break this implementation?
Back: The left neighbor would still contain the previous row’s value rather than the current row’s solved cost.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for minimum_grid_cost. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Every route into a cell has a final move from above or left. Minimizing over those optimal prefixes gives the best route to that cell. Row-major order solves both dependencies before their values are needed.

Front: Tries: organize information by shared prefixes: Does a prefix count of 2 prove the prefix itself was inserted?
Back: No. Two longer strings may share that prefix without the prefix being a complete inserted word.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for PrefixIndex. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Each insertion increments precisely the nodes corresponding to its prefixes, including the empty prefix at the root. Therefore a reached node’s count equals the number of entries matching that prefix. A missing edge means zero matches.

Front: Disjoint sets for growing connectivity: Can parent pointers reconstruct the original connecting edges?
Back: No. Union and compression change the representation; it is not the original graph.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for DisjointSets. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Each parent tree represents exactly one connected group. Joining representatives merges exactly two groups and cannot create an internal parent cycle. Compression changes a node’s parent only to another ancestor in the same group.

Front: Weighted routes and Dijkstra’s frontier: Why can a negative edge invalidate a settled distance?
Back: A later route could reduce its total after reaching a farther vertex, contradicting the nondecreasing frontier argument.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for shortest_costs. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: When the smallest current tentative distance is popped, an undiscovered shorter route would have to pass through a frontier vertex with no greater distance. Nonnegative edges prevent such a route from appearing later. Relaxing outgoing edges preserves shortest known route costs.

Front: Bits and representation contracts: What is the answer when a equals b?
Back: Zero, because their XOR is zero and the loop runs zero times.

Front: Explain the correctness argument for differing_bits. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: XOR selects precisely the differing positions. Each clearing iteration removes exactly one selected position and leaves all others unchanged. The number of iterations equals the desired count.

Front: A complete interview: clarify, derive, test: What does [5, 5, 5] with duration 1 return?
Back: 3. All three distinct events fit in [5,6).

Front: Explain the correctness argument for busiest_span. Recall its lesson exercise first.
Back: Every valid set of contiguous events has spread less than duration and can be covered by a half-open interval starting at its first event. Shrinking removes exactly the left endpoints whose spread is too large for the current right endpoint. Taking the maximum over all right endpoints covers an optimal set.
